newsitem.title: GERMANY: Schaeuble sees little hope of German tax deal soon.
newsitem.headline: Schaeuble sees little hope of German tax deal soon.

text.p: A leading figure in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's German coalition said on Tuesday there was barely any chance of reaching an early compromise with the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) on sweeping tax reforms.
Wolfgang Schaeuble, tax negotiator for Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), told the Die Zeit weekly the two sides would probably end up thrashing out a compromise on government later in parliament.

"We are ready to meet the SPD for talks at any time during the Easter break. Otherwise we will meet each other again in the mediation committee," Schaeuble said in an interview due for publication on Wednesday.

The SPD controls the upper house of parliament and can block most tax measures. Parliament's mediation process offers the chance to thrash out a compromise if legislation is voted down -- something that Schaeuble said he expected.
"It looks like that. The performance the Social Democrats are putting on over tax reforms is hardly even funny any more," he said.
Schaeuble is one of the architects of a package of 30 billion marks in tax cuts drawn up under Finance Minister Theo Waigel which would be implemented in 1998 and 1999.
Legislation for the first, smaller, round of cuts was introduced in parliament at the final pre-Easter session. Big income and corporate tax cuts to take effect in 1999 will also be launched soon.

Stung by record post-war unemployment, both sides had begun a dialogue on taxes, but talks have been suspended since the SPD walked out in a row over coal subsidies. Each has blamed the other for turning down invitations to resume the talks.

Schaeuble said it was vital to reduce state spending in order to create jobs, but he ruled out the kind of radical policy solutions pursued by the United States and Britain in the 1980s. -- Bonn newsroom, 49-228-26097150
